title: Celebrity Culture Predicted Fertility Decline in Japan and South Korea
author: Peter Foreshaw Brookes and Lyman Stone
source: Institute for Family Studies (ifstudies.org), November 3, 2026, November 6, 2026
summary: Peter Foreshaw Brookes and Lyman Stone argue that Japan's unusually persistent fertility decline from the mid-1980s is better explained by a distinctive celebrity culture than by the usual economic story. They note that Japan's early-1970s downturn tracked Western trends, that economic shocks rarely trigger decades-long declines, and that the 1990s crisis did not accelerate the trend. What set Japan apart was the satellite-TV-driven idol culture, in which stars were expected to be emotionally available and to hide romantic and family life. That norm encourages parasocial attachments while depriving the public of role models for relationships and parenthood. The authors test the theory in South Korea, where fertility began falling just after idol culture arrived in 1992 and showed no break around the 1997 financial crisis. Their Baby Nudges survey found Japan and Korea had the highest rates of admiring public figures with no children, and they suggest that familistic celebrities and policy nudges might help.
points: Japan's fertility decline from the mid-1980s matches the rise of idol culture better than economic shocks such as the oil crisis, the Plaza Accords or housing costs.
Idol culture asked celebrities to hide romance and family, encouraging parasocial bonds while removing visible models of family life.
South Korea's fertility decline began soon after Japanese-style idol culture arrived in 1992 and did not turn at the 1997 crisis.
Survey data show Japanese and Korean respondents most often admire public figures without children, and admiring a celebrity with a bigger family raised intent to have another child by 14%.
Governments might nudge toward celebrities who model family life instead of, as in Korea, promoting childless stars.
quotes: Sometimes, a fertility trend change that looks like it was prompted by economic factors turns out to have important cultural elements, too.
Economic conditions do affect fertility, but we generally don’t tend to see a single economic shock precipitating a downward fertility trend for decades.
Distinct from Western celebrities, Japanese celebrities were routinely expected to appear emotionally available and minimize discussion of their personal romantic and family life

The pernicious result of this norm is that the populace at large is simultaneously encouraged to develop parasocial relationships with celebrities (which may compete with their own relationships) and deprived of role modeling of romantic and family life by those with whom they have such parasocial relationships.

Sure enough, the South Korean fertility rate began to decline immediately following the beginning of Japan-style celebrity idol culture in the early 1990s, and showed no immediate trend break in the late 1990s around a major economic crisis.
Japan and Korea reported the highest rates of admiring a public figure with no record of having children.
The Japanese and Korean examples provide further suggestive evidence that visible engagement with family life by cultural leaders matters for fertility.
Could other governments establish nudges to generate familistic celebrities instead? We think it might be possible.
